ChIJ0T0PbtwjVIgRO88RijZvjJs.desc: A unique and charming historic event venue in the heart of Mint Hill. Host your wedding or special event at The Barn in the Village.
ChIJ0T0PbtwjVIgRO88RijZvjJs.home: There's no place like The Barn & The Village. We hosted our rehearsal dinner on the grounds and it was perfection. So unique and so warm...a great way to make our guests feel at home in our hometown.
ChIJ0T0PbtwjVIgRO88RijZvjJs.about: The Barn is a culmination of time, talents, and love from the Mint Hill Community. It is our most fervent hope that The Barn will become a backdrop for our community's most special events. A place to feel a bit of history underneath your feet. The Barn in the Carl J. McEwen Historic Village was originally erected near the village of Bellville, Ohio more than 125 years ago. It was constructed with mortise and tenon connections pegged with hand hewn wooden pegs into solid wood piles and beams. The beams are beautiful elm, the rafters are red oak, and connections are both red and white oak. Farmers used whatever was available near the site and it was not uncommon for several types of wood to be used on a single barn. Neighbors helped neighbors build. Barns were essential. When The Barn arrived at the Carl J. McEwen Historic Village in 2020, volunteers got to work. The spirit of neighbors helping neighbors continued 125 years later. Volunteers stained boards using 30 gallons of stain, nailed thousands of nails, and collectively spent too many hours to count making this barn a special place. It is now an urban chic gem. ChIJ28596kNzVIgRP64tDp_JACc.about: The Andrews Farm located in Midland, North Carolina has been a part of the Andrews family since the 1970’s. As a third generation family farm there is an abundance of history which has evolved over the years. Originally the land was used for the sole purpose of farming wheat, soybeans, corn and cotton. Over time the farm evolved into something much more meaningful to our family. In the early 1990’s a cabin dating back to the late 1700’s was discovered on the property and the family decided to restore it and use it as a place to gather on weekends and holidays. As a result, the farm became a place the entire family could enjoy while having the privileges of experiencing the gifts this beautiful land offers. Some of our family members have loved the farm experience so much that they chose to move to the farm permanently building the home, a modern European inspired farmhouse, that sits on the venue ground’s today. Many joyous occasions and unforgettable memories have transpired on the Andrews farm over the past fifty years including birthday parties, oyster roasts, dove hunts and Thanksgiving dinners. After hosting many large events over the years, the Andrews family is thrilled to now be able to offer this special gem to others as a wedding and special events venue starting in 2020. We would be remiss if we didn’t honor those who paved the way for us to be at this exact moment we are today. Milas Safrit and his wife acquired the farmland through his wife’s family in the late 1800’s. One of their children, Grover Safrit, bought the current farm around 1916 and cut timber from the land to build the house that remains on the farm today. He was a truck farmer producing fruits & vegetables. Ray Safrit was one of Grover’s sons and took ownership of the farm, along with his wife Phyllis, around 1963 when he bought his first cow. Ray was the first farmer to bring Beefmasters to this area of the Carolinas. Many of our family & friends remember Ray on his big green tractor or tending to his beloved garden. The transition to regenerative farming began in the late 80’s and early 90s as Danny Safrit, Ray’s son, started learning about Management Intensive Grazing. Danny, an engineer by trade, has worked on the farm throughout his life and would travel during his college years to help his dad tend to the farm animals. ChIJA6jVNxaRVogRUTttSgS-du4.about: Nova Initia means “New Beginnings” in Latin. That name wasn’t created in a brainstorm session. It came during one of the most difficult seasons of my life. On October 20, 2017, my mother passed away. At the time, I was working a full-time job while quietly building what I hoped would become a real production company. I had already started the transition — investing in gear, taking on projects, trying to step into something bigger. But grief has a way of slowing everything down. The original business name I wanted — based on my initials — was already taken. And in the middle of navigating loss, uncertainty, and the pressure of building something from scratch, I found myself questioning what this next chapter was supposed to look like. During a conversation with a coworker about possible names, she mentioned Nova Initia — Latin for “New Beginnings.” Because that’s exactly what that season felt like. Not a clean slate. Not a perfect restart. But a forced turning of the page. A moment where grief, legacy, and ambition were colliding. Nova Initia became more than a name. It became a commitment. A commitment to honor where I came from. A commitment to build something meaningful. A commitment to help others tell the stories that mark their own turning points. ChIJA4KLb5GvVogRGT5pwXQIh7I.home: A beautiful event venue on 11 acres of farmland just north of Charlotte, in Huntersville NC. Our property is conveniently located just 4 miles from a plethora of hotels and restaurants as well as interstate 77. With a rich history and charming character, The Ivory Barn is the perfect place to start your forever. The barn is a 5000 sq ft temperature-controlled modern building with two stylish dressing suites, a classy built-in bar space, posh bathrooms, and a caterer's warming kitchen. The main event space in the barn is wide open and has charming features, tall ceilings, and a wall of windows, giving guests meadow views, and lots of natural light. Outside, on the meadow end of the barn, is a large patio where you can host an al fresco cocktail hour under the bistro lights. Our covered pavilion, with its greenhouse inspired design, is a lovely spot for friends and family to witness the exchange of vows. The gas fire pit is a gathering spot when the sun goes down, and the old red hay barn will be the perfect backdrop for photos.
ChIJA4KLb5GvVogRGT5pwXQIh7I.about: We are Kevin and Gayle, owners of The Ivory Barn. Kevin and I have been married for 25 years and have two adult children that we raised right here in Huntersville. When our youngest graduated high school and was leaving for college, we started to dream about what our next chapter would look like. After hosting many parties at the property we live on, we were often told, "You guys could host weddings back here." My thought was always, that would be a dream. There is something about creating a setting, so that people can gather together to make memories, that hits me in the heart. Kevin, never shying away from hard work, was on board. So we decided to explore the idea. On the weekends, we would go to Starbucks with our notebook and an iPad to brainstorm about what an event venue would look like for us. A couple months later we were looking for land and a few months after that we had our property under contract. Here we are, a few years later, standing in the event space we have envisioned, a place our community will be proud of. We look forward to spending the next chapter of our lives seeing people here dancing and singing, hugging and laughing, and we can't wait!

ChIJH1BcXm-KVogRO6gTKmsH2vU.about: The Robertson House is a fine reminder of the large number of 19th-century structures of handsome proportion and quality construction that once dotted York County. It originally stood proudly on the corner of Robertson and Ogden Roads. Today this is the location of the SC Department of Transportation, and nothing remains but the family cemetery. By the early 1970s, the house was unoccupied and beginning to show signs of significant deterioration. Dr. Frank Fairey, a Rock Hill surgeon, had an intense interest in historical artifacts and the preservation of history. He took notice of the home and its lovely lines, eyebrow windows, panel doors, elegant wainscoting, shouldered brick chimneys, and original window glass. One day, as he was driving by the house, a large red fire truck was sitting in the driveway. The officials touring the home told him they had no desire to save the house, and in fact, were going to burn it down for a fire training exercise. Within a few days, the Fairey family purchased an option on the Robertson House from the owners, the City of Rock Hill. In the 1980s, Dr. Fairey and his wife, Martha, moved the beautiful house from its original location on Robertson Road to Oak Park Road where it now sits overlooking Fishing Creek. ChIJIaeFsNf_U4gRw1UZtqsUgNo.about: Espy Watts Brawley founded the Estate in the early 1900s. The home was ordered from Sears and Roebuck, back when you ordered homes from catalogs. It was shipped to Mooresville by train and assembled on site piece by piece. The Brawley Family transformed the spacious land with a little bit of elbow grease into their charming home and decided to call it Lawndale. Mr. Brawley was never one to sit idle, running the bank and starting a flour mill in Mooresville. The flour mill still runs today and produces all the flour for a southern donut company that we all know and love. Unfortunately, over the years, the house went into disrepair. But, it was added to the national historical registry as a historical site. At the turn of the century, the current owners were inspired by the Brawley’s family story, and purchased the property. They wanted to stay true to the Brawley’s love for their family. Using that same elbow grease that inspired the first home, they restored the Estate to its former glory and built the pavilion as an event space to bring their friends and family to come together. As their family grew up, they needed to partner with a professional management company. La-Tea-Da’s was the perfect company to embrace the charm of the Estate. For me, photography has always been about so much more than beautiful images—it's about people. I have a deep passion for preserving life's most meaningful moments, from the excitement of your wedding day to the quiet joy of welcoming a new baby or celebrating the milestones that shape your family's story. My hope is that years from now, you'll look back through your photographs and be transported to those moments all over again, remembering the love, the laughter, and the people who made them so special. It is an honor to preserve those memories for you and your family for generations to come. I wasn’t always a photographer, but I always knew I wanted to connect with people. My love for photography began long before I ever imagined owning a business. As a kid, I was always the one with a camera in my hands. I spent countless hours capturing everyday moments with my friends and family, first with Polaroids in elementary school and later with my very first digital camera in middle school. Looking back, I realize I wasn't just taking pictures—I was preserving memories. Growing up, I dreamed of becoming a National Geographic photographer. ChIJV5HZ4tKOVogRioG-m5VKrNM.about: Digital Spark created the brand film for Tritium Power Solutions, the EV charger manufacturer introducing itself as a new company since September 2024. Tritium Power Solutions was established in September 2024, a new company built on twenty years of EV charging expertise under new ownership and new leadership. The film had to introduce that company on its own terms: not a comeback story, a new one. It had to prove the engineering is real, the manufacturing is real, and the support behind every charger is real, in a fast trailer cut and in a fuller sit-down version, for different moments of a buyer's attention. We shot on the manufacturing floor in Tennessee, where the product is actually made, timed the visit to overlap with a customer already touring the plant, and let the interviews run off the cuff instead of scripted. A trailer cut carries the pace and the sound design; the full film goes deeper into the engineering, the manufacturing, and the support behind the warranty once someone is already watching. A Different Approach To Wedding Photography
ChIJXVpMgFGcuiURdU8-Xprmq74.home: For couples that want their wedding captured honestly . You don't need a photographer who wants to be your best friend. You need one who knows how to tell the truth about your day. I'm Brandon — a documentary wedding photographer in Charlotte. I'm not going to pretend the process leading up to your wedding needs to be some elaborate experience. Booking with me is simple: we talk, we plan what actually matters, and then I get out of your way so you can be present for your own day instead of managing mine. On the day itself, my job is to pay attention — closely, and without getting in the middle of things. I want the photos to feel emotionally true to what happened, not staged around what looks good. I do care about making images that are artistically strong. I just won't chase that at the expense of what's real and what is best for my clients. The story comes first. Every time. Based in Charlotte, NC . Photographing weddings anywhere in the U.S A Different Approach To Wedding Photography I want my couples to actually enjoy their wedding day. I'll give direction if it's useful, but 98% of your wedding is photographed as it actually happened—the people, the quiet moments, the chaos, the things you planned and the things you couldn't. Because years from now, I think you'll want to remember more than what everything looked like. You'll want to remember what it felt like to be there. If you want a photographer who'll pose you against every wall on the property, or re-create photos you found on Pinterest, there are excellent photographers in Charlotte who do exactly that — genuinely, go find one, you'll be happy. If instead you want someone who disappears into the day and hands you back what really happened, that's the job I'm built for. St. Mathew Catholic Church & Reid House

I came to photography because I liked paying attention. The things most people overlook. The person standing just outside the group. A parent watching from across the room. Lisa's father, Terry, was up to the challenge and had been thinking of building a barn for himself to store all of the antique's he had collected over the years as well as his farm equipment. And so, construction began. The 4,000 square foot barn was built entirely by Terry, Lisa, Ben, and two carpenters. (Yes, just 5 people!) Construction took approximately a year to complete. The main structure is comprised of cedar trees that were cut along the creek on the property. Sticking with the cedar theme, the exterior siding and inside walls are made of rough cut cedar... all trees that were locally grown and cut. After Lisa & Ben's wedding, while the couple were on their honeymoon in Italy, Lisa began to get inquiries from old high school friends about renting the venue for their own special day. ChIJaWIp7yovVIgRBvOG75YXAQs.about: In 1982, I began DJing in skating rinks and then nightclubs in Buffalo NY. A family friend helped me to create the name Sonic Sounds. When I was married, I realized that I no longer wanted to DJ in the clubs so I bought my own equipment and began to mobile DJ at weddings and parties around Western New York. When I moved to Charlotte in 1996, I began to actively seek out clients. The rest, as they say, is history. --- Reginald Sutton (Co-owner of Sonic Sounds) Music is big in our family. Each of my 3 children learned at a very young age that when Daddy had to DJ, they needed to carry something. This actually occurred around age 4 for each of them. They became “roadies” and would help with set-up and take-down. They also began to recognize song names and artists and were able to quickly make suggestions for what to play next. My wife types up all of the contracts, takes care of mailings, and is also a “roadie”. When we are doing a pool party, everyone in the family is involved with running games and distributing prizes. My oldest son began to be interested in how to DJ when he was in 5th grade. He now has become an assistant as well as a DJ when I am double-booked. --- Reginald Sutton (Co-owner of Sonic Sounds)

Welcome to The Woman’s Club of Rock Hill, a warm, caring network of women who come together to serve, connect, and make a difference right here in Rock Hill. Our club is proud to call the historic Armstrong-Mauldin House and Mauldin Gardens home. Whether through service or celebration, we invite you to connect with us and experience the spirit of The Woman’s Club of Rock Hill, a 501c3 organization. ChIJezByWPuIVogR9jdDGDEjLR0.about: The two-story home of Spanish and American Colonial style at 607 Aiken Avenue was built in 1921 by renowned, regional architect A.D. Gilchrist for Rock Hill Mayor, W.R. Armstrong. Design characteristics of the 4,000-square-foot home include a low-pitched roof, clay roof tiles, a square, symmetrical façade, and surface decorations in low relief. Local businessman William M. Mauldin purchased the home for his family in 1923. The house was knownbriefly as the “Coca-Cola House.” Mauldin had purchased the Rock Hill Coca-Cola Plant in 1908 and, with it, the exclusive right to bottle and sell Coca-Cola to customers in Rock Hill and the surrounding counties. ChIJg8Ro6VqhVogR6uxuReQ6pQk.about: About Us Our Purpose History Art Gallery The Grace Community Residents Community Engagement Memberships News & Ideas In the News Collectively Speaking For nearly 80 years, the land now occupied by the Government Center in Uptown Charlotte was a thriving predominantly black community. In the late 1860s, recently-emancipated slaves gathered in the neighborhood, known colloquially as “Logtown” before it was a considered a neighborhood, and over the years the community would become a self-sustaining “city within a city” for Charlotte’s black residents with churches, schools, and businesses independent of those outside the neighborhood, where Charlotte’s black residents were not welcome at white institutions. Residents came to know the neighborhood as “Brooklyn'', an homage to the New York City borough. The community grew as Charlotte’s black families were pushed from other communities during segregation, and the black community was forced to build its own institutions. Some of these included the Myers Street School, opened in 1886, which was Charlotte’s first black public school, as well as the city of Charlotte’s first black YMCA. The library that sat on Brevard Street was the first free library in the state of North Carolina for black residents. ChIJietLaCCgVogRud59BBTDOSc.about: In 1914 a Sunday school mission congregation hired a prominent Charlotte architect to build them a new church home. The men, women and children gathered, prayed and wed in the neoclassical church for nearly 70 years. In the late 1980s, the church was faced with a declining membership and a dramatically changing neighborhood. After much thought and prayer, the congregation opted to keep the church alive by moving to the suburbs. In 1997 the property was purchased by a local businessman and philanthropist who christened it the Great Aunt Stella Center, after a beloved great aunt who was a home missionary and advocate for the poor. The Center was reborn as one of Charlotte’s more interesting arts and cultural venues. The Center became a prime setting for music performances, lectures, debates and conferences. The education building, built in 1925, has served as home to several non-profit organizations and a charter school. A local church, Uptown Church, continues to hold services every Sunday. Hundreds of brides discovered the simple beauty of the circular sanctuary and the Italian stained glass windows. In the summer of 2002, Self-Help, an affiliate of one of the nation’s leading community development financial institutions, purchased the property. It’s one of the most unique wedding venues in Charlotte! The garden is open to the general public. Come take a casual stroll, have a picnic, or relax on your favorite bench. We do close for weddings. Please view our calendar before planning your visit! Coffee and wine in a garden? Yes, please! Learn more about Rosie’s Coffee & Wine.
ChIJjbcWSBegVogRRHSQeejXhJA.about: Henry McGill purchased the Avant Fuel & Ice Company in 1950. In an attempt to beautify the urban and industrial plot of land, Henry’s wife, Helen, shared her love for gardening and started planting rose bushes along the fence line. Over the years, more than 500 rose bushes were planted, and the garden became a spectacle to behold. On Mother’s Day, 1967, the McGill Rose Garden opened to the public as a space for the community to enjoy the roses, greenery, and nature in an otherwise urban area. To this day, Mother’s Day is still a popular day for the community to visit and has become a tradition for many families. In addition to the variety of plants and hidden paths you’ll find in the garden, you’ll also find a 34-ton coal hopper from the Seaboard Railroad Company. It was donated in memory of Helen McGill and is not only a conversation piece but a reminder of the beauty she contributed to the area. In 1976, the Avant Fuel & Ice Company closed its doors, and the garden was sold to the City of Charlotte. The McGill Rose Garden then became a public city park, available for all to enjoy, and has welcomed the community to host weddings, photoshoots, baby showers, and various events for years. The small brick building on site is now occupied by Rosie’s Coffee & Wine, but has also been home to a variety of businesses, including Rosie’s sister company, Nectar , a boutique floral studio.

ChIJkXqAcYsfVIgRXJmM9aPYglY.home: Charlotte, NC Wedding & Portrait Photographer I'm not new here—Charlotte is my hometown, and for over 23 years, I’ve had the joy of capturing weddings and portraits across this vibrant city and beyond. As a seasoned professional photographer, I’ve had the privilege of working alongside many of Charlotte’s most trusted vendors and have photographed love stories in nearly every local church and reception venue you can name. Being a native means I know the ins and outs of this city—the hidden gems, golden-hour skyline spots, and the perfect backdrops for every kind of session. Whether you need a recommendation for a top-tier florist, a talented makeup artist, or a dreamy location for your family portraits, I'm here to help. Consider me your friendly and knowledgeable guide and collaborator from start to finish. Though Charlotte will always be home, my camera and I have traveled far and wide—from the Blue Ridge Mountains to the Carolina coasts and throughout the eastern U.S., Mexico, Spain, and Australia—capturing moments with authenticity, artistry, and heart. I proudly serve all couples and families and am deeply committed to creating an inclusive, affirming space where everyone feels seen and celebrated. LGBTQIA+ love stories, chosen families, and all expressions of identity are not just welcomed—they're embraced with open arms and a full heart. Let’s make something beautiful together. Please get in touch here and let me know what you've got in mind.
ChIJkXqAcYsfVIgRXJmM9aPYglY.about: I picked up a camera in high school and fell hard. I’d taken pictures before—on simple 35mm Kodaks and rainbow-striped Polaroids—but when I began learning the technical and artistic language of photography as a teenager, something clicked. I was captivated by the way photographs hold time—how they preserve moments that often pass far too quickly, and yet come to mean everything. That sense of awe has never left me. I continued photographing through college and earned my credential in photography from the Creative Circus in Atlanta in 2002. I founded Piper Warlick Photography that same year and have been photographing portraits and weddings ever since. Over more than two decades, I’ve been entrusted with moments both ordinary and extraordinary—quiet milestones and once-in-a-lifetime days. My work has grown as I have, shaped by experience, curiosity, and a deep respect for the people who invite me into their lives. At the heart of everything I do is a genuine love of people. I proudly serve individuals, couples, and families of every race, faith, gender identity, sexual orientation, and background. Creating an affirming, respectful space—where people feel seen and at ease—is not an add-on to my work. It is foundational. What I cherish most is the moment someone reaches out and tells me who they are right now. Graduating. Becoming parents. Grieving a loss. Claiming their identity.

ChIJp3SlQKqhVogRoVTZDanY9dc.about: Rosie, our beloved shop cat at the McGill Rose Garden for a little over four years, claimed the rose garden as her own one morning in May of 2012. She quickly became the real boss around here, and no one came or went without a thorough once-over from Rosie. She was sassy and spunky, had a very big attitude, and we miss her dearly. Unfortunately, she unexpectedly passed away in 2017, but she lives on in our hearts and in the tons of photographs that were taken of her. We talk and laugh about all of her antics still today. So, we felt it was only fitting to raise a glass to a departed member of our “family” and name our wine and coffee garden after her. So if you knew Rosie, just heard about her, or maybe saw her image on social media, come by and reminisce a little bit. Of course, if you didn’t know Rosie, we still want you to stop by, grab a coffee, a beer, or a glass of wine, and stroll through the garden to see where Rosie used to frolic. (But let’s be serious, she just laid around a lot). Come gather with friends in a really cool spot, relax, and enjoy yourself. We look forward to seeing everyone soon!

While the upper floors are now home to The View Apartments, the lower level has been transformed into the wedding venue we proudly call home, providing couples with a timeless setting steeped in history and charm. ChIJsdfIngGJVogRjXYpTcipaYQ.about: Historic Rock Hill was founded more than thirty years ago as the volunteer organization The Midtown Preservation Society. Today, we are still in the business of preservation, but as a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization. We work to preserve not only the buildings in Rock Hill, but the stories of Rock Hill. Our passion lies in ensuring that ALL stories are told and preserved, even the stories that are sometimes difficult to tell. Historic Rock Hill owns the Historic White Home which acts as a community and events venue as well as a historical site that tells the story of the White family and their growth alongside the city of Rock Hill. What started as a one-room cabin on the lands of the Catawba Indian Nation grew to the large Reconstruction Era home you see today. From family farm to boarding house to stately home, the White Home has stood firm as Rock Hill has grown up around it. The woman who built the house, Ann White, wielded her influence in the growing town, bringing a school to the area, as well as donating land for use for the First Presbyterian Church. Tours of the historic home show how this simple farmhouse has stood the test of time. HRH helps tell the story of the men who built the home, the woman who independently raised her family and ran a successful business, and the town that has grown into the thriving community we live in today. ChIJu_6uwa62VogR55Nqke2Q_r4.about: The home known as Vesuvius proudly sits as the oldest standing home in Lincoln County. Built in 1792 by General Joseph Graham, Vesuvius has seen over 200 years of American history. Located on the property are the remnants of the iron furnace built by Graham in 1795. This was one of the first of many furnaces built in Lincoln county that helped to produce many different types of iron works well into the 1800’s. Joseph Graham and his family played a big role in North Carolina politics and industry. Most notably, his son William Graham served as Governor of North Carolina, Secretary of the Navy, and was a vice President candidate. The home is on the National Historic Registry listing and still maintains most of its original structure and architecture. In 2007 renovations on the home began. The first wedding was hosted in July of 2009 for Jay and his wife Kristy who you now see working behind the scenes at every event. Our vision for preserving this home and creating a beautiful event venue on this historic property was now a reality. Since that day, Vesuvius has seen more than 300 weddings as well as countless other events.
